title: ASIC reveals bad actor hit-list
full_text:
Artificial intelligence can make decisions, but companies cannot blame the chatbots, the corporate regulator will warn, as it revealed plans to focus on technological havoc in the heart of financial markets.
Policing AI and how firms are using the new technology will form a key plank of the Australian Securities & Investments Commission’s enforcement agenda in the year ahead.
Revealing its enforcement priorities on Wednesday, ASIC will say AI can be used but it cannot alter legal obligations.
Indeed, ASIC chair Sarah Court will warn companies they must leave open an angle for customers to obtain a human review, particularly when they seek to make a complaint, respond to a scam, make an insurance claim, or seek financial assistance.
“ASIC will focus on poorly designed or inadequately supervised systems that produce misleading information, make inappropriate decisions or prevent customers from accessing effective support and assistance,” Ms Court will say.
“The technology may be new. The responsibility is not.” Ms Court will say that ASIC is focused on the “serious failures” in how technology is used by companies to make inappropriate decisions.
Her speech comes as firms within the financial sector double down on the use of AI, as banks cut staff with plans to replace their roles firstly offshore and later with AI agents.
Recently, NAB, led by Andrew Irvine, announced it would slash 2500 jobs, moving most of the roles overseas. Qantas will cut 850 jobs, with many to eventually be replaced with AI.
ASIC will map out its nine areas of interest, domains the regulator will focus its enforcement activity on in the coming year ahead.
ASIC said it was focused on misconduct that adds to the cost-of-living pressures.
The regulator will pursue banks, insurers and superannuation funds that make promises around pricing, discounts, or entitlements, but cannot deliver.
Already ASIC has extracted $570m in fines from major companies over the past 12 months of enforcement activity.
ASIC also recommitted to acting on the Shield and First Guardian Master Fund scandals, which have entrapped the retiree savings of thousands of people.
The regulator also said it was looking at issues exposed by the failures of the funds, probing conflicted financial advice, the lead generation sector, and how they tied into private credit and managed investment schemes.
On Tuesday ASIC announced it was running a review of private credit, after wrapping up a recent round, with hopes to examine how lenders have responded to its push on valuations and fees. The private credit sector is grappling with the blow-up of homebuilder Bathla, which tapped credit lenders for $3.6bn in loans. Ms Court will say funds must “uplift standards”.
